item.title: PM Rabuka to skip PIF Leaders Meeting in Palau
item.description: Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka will not attend the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting in Palau, with Foreign Affairs Minister Sakiasi Ditoka set to represent Fiji. The Forum Leaders Meeting, which is being held in Palau, is expected to be an important platform for Pacific leaders to strengthen regional cooperation and agree on common priorities ahead of Pre-COP31 and COP31.
item.content:encoded:
Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka will not attend the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting in Palau, with Foreign Affairs Minister Sakiasi Ditoka set to represent Fiji.

The Forum Leaders Meeting, which is being held in Palau, is expected to be an important platform for Pacific leaders to strengthen regional cooperation and agree on common priorities ahead of Pre-COP31 and COP31.

Fiji’s delegation will be led by Mr Ditoka, while Minister for Information, Environment and Climate Change and PSIDS Chair Lynda Tabuya has highlighted climate change as one of Fiji’s key priorities at the meeting.

Ms Tabuya said Fiji wants Pacific leaders to endorse the region’s key climate priorities through the Belau Declaration ahead of Pre-COP31.

“Palau is where we build the political mandate. Pre-COP is where we take it to the world,” she said.

She said the Pacific’s position was clear — keeping the 1.5°C target alive, securing accessible climate finance, protecting the ocean and recognising the special circumstances of Pacific Small Island Developing States.

Ms Tabuya said the outcomes of climate negotiations directly affect the lives of ordinary Pacific Islanders, including coastal protection, farmers recovering from disasters, access to clean water and the sustainability of fisheries.

The Pacific position will also include the voices of young people through the Regional Council of Youth Declaration.

“Our young people will inherit the consequences of the decisions we make. Their voice belongs in our Pacific position,” Ms Tabuya said.

As PSIDS Chair, she said Pacific unity remained the region’s greatest negotiating strength.

“We contribute the least to this crisis but carry some of its greatest impacts. The Belau Declaration must give us a clear mandate to carry from Palau to Pre-COP31 and on to COP31.”

Fiji will host Pre-COP31 in October, ahead of COP31, giving the Pacific an opportunity to take its priorities directly to the global climate negotiations.

item.title: Audit finds weak controls at Tavua Town Council
item.description: Weak internal controls at the Tavua Town Council increased the risk of fraud, potential misappropriation of funds and inaccurate financial reporting, according to the Auditor-General’s Report on Municipal Councils recently tabled in Parliament. The Auditor-General issued a modified – qualified opinion on the council’s financial statements covering the 2021 to 2023 financial years.
item.content:encoded:
Weak internal controls at the Tavua Town Council increased the risk of fraud, potential misappropriation of funds and inaccurate financial reporting, according to the Auditor-General’s Report on Municipal Councils recently tabled in Parliament.

The Auditor-General issued a modified – qualified opinion on the council’s financial statements covering the 2021 to 2023 financial years.

Among the weaknesses identified was the council’s failure to prepare monthly bank reconciliation statements between January and July 2022.

The audit also found there was no bank audit certificate for one of the council’s accounts, while an undeposited amount of $430 appearing in a bank reconciliation statement could not be verified because subsequent bank statements were not provided.

Physical counts of council assets were not periodically conducted and assets were not tagged, while weaknesses were also identified in revenue management.

“These control weaknesses increase the risk of fraud, potential misappropriation of funds, and incorrect financial reporting,” the report stated.

The audit also raised concerns over the council’s VAT records.

Tavua Town Council was unable to provide VAT reconciliations supporting payable balances of $38,226 in 2021 and $38,695 in 2022.

For 2023, auditors were unable to verify a further VAT payable balance of $18,001 because reconciliation statements and supporting documents were not provided.

Questions were also raised over the council’s treatment of government grants and deferred income.

The report found the council had not complied with relevant financial reporting requirements in recognising government grants and had failed to disclose certain unfulfilled conditions attached to grants.

Auditors were also unable to fully verify market fees, public convenience income and rates.

Unreconciled differences of $9,086 in 2021 and $4,995 in 2022 were identified between the rates listing and financial statements.

A further $8,345 variance was identified between the disclosed compensation for key management personnel and supporting information supplied by the council.

The audit said this prevented it from determining whether the reported key management compensation of $43,704 was fairly disclosed.

The findings form part of the Auditor-General’s broader examination of financial reporting and governance across Fiji’s municipal councils.

item.title: CRC to submit final Constitution Review Report today
item.description: Fiji’s constitutional review process reaches a major milestone today when the Constitutional Review Commission (CRC) submits its final report to President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu. The report marks the culmination of months of nationwide consultations, with the Commission travelling across the country to hear directly from Fijians about the Constitution and their vision for Fiji’s constitutional fu
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s constitutional review process reaches a major milestone today when the Constitutional Review Commission (CRC) submits its final report to President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu.

The report marks the culmination of months of nationwide consultations, with the Commission travelling across the country to hear directly from Fijians about the Constitution and their vision for Fiji’s constitutional future.

Communities, villages, organisations, institutions and other stakeholders took part in the consultations, presenting their views, concerns, aspirations and recommendations.

The CRC’s submission will formally bring its extensive consultation process to an end and pave the way for the next stage of the constitutional review.

Attention will now shift to the Commission’s findings and recommendations, and how these will be considered as Fiji moves forward with the constitutional process.

The submission is expected to be a significant moment in what could become an important chapter in Fiji’s constitutional history.

item.title: PM Rabuka accused of using Navua town status as campaign stunt
item.description: Chaudhry says the FLP acknowledges that Navua residents have waited a long time for town status, but questions whether the necessary groundwork for municipal governance has been completed. “The problem is that the Prime Minister has made the announcement while the basic work of a town remains unfinished,” Chaudhry said.
item.content:encoded:
Chaudhry says the FLP acknowledges that Navua residents have waited a long time for town status, but questions whether the necessary groundwork for municipal governance has been completed.

“The problem is that the Prime Minister has made the announcement while the basic work of a town remains unfinished,” Chaudhry said.

He questioned why the town boundary had not been publicly released, saying residents needed to know the extent of the township, which properties would fall within it and who would be required to pay rates.

Chaudhry also questioned whether a special administrator had been appointed and called for clarity on the town’s budget, planning scheme and services.

“A town cannot function on a declaration alone. It needs an authority in place, a budget, a town planning scheme, and a clear list of services,” he said.

He said Navua’s biggest challenge remained flooding, given its location along the Navua River and its history of repeated inundation.

Chaudhry said drainage, river management and flood protection must be treated as core municipal responsibilities.

He also raised concerns over the timing of the declaration, noting that local government elections had already been deferred until after the general election.

“In that setting, a late declaration without a completed planning scheme, a working administrator and visible services looks more like campaign timing than grounded local government reform,” he said.

The FLP is calling on the Prime Minister and Minister for Local Government to publish Navua’s town boundary, confirm whether a special administrator is in place and outline the services the new municipality will deliver during its first year.

“Navua deserves proper municipal government, not a ceremony,” Chaudhry said.

item.title: Auditor-General raises major concerns over Nausori Town Council accounts
item.description: The Auditor-General was unable to verify millions of dollars in financial balances at the Nausori Town Council after finding significant gaps in records and supporting documentation covering the 2019 to 2021 financial years. The concerns are detailed in the Report of the Auditor-General on Municipal Councils, recently tabled in Parliament, which records a modified – disclaimer of opinion for Nauso
item.content:encoded:
The Auditor-General was unable to verify millions of dollars in financial balances at the Nausori Town Council after finding significant gaps in records and supporting documentation covering the 2019 to 2021 financial years.

The concerns are detailed in the Report of the Auditor-General on Municipal Councils, recently tabled in Parliament, which records a modified – disclaimer of opinion for Nausori Town Council.

The report said auditors could not obtain sufficient and appropriate evidence to verify opening balances and determine their impact on subsequent financial statements.

Among the issues identified were the way the council recorded its cash transactions.

The report said receipts and payments were entered into the cash general ledger using bank statements rather than original source documents such as receipt books.

It also found transactions from one of the council’s bank accounts were not recorded in its accounts, while a register for cancelled and stale cheques was not maintained and cheque books were not provided for audit.

Significant concerns were also raised over millions of dollars in receivables.

The council reported Trade and Other Receivables of $3 million in 2019, $3.02 million in 2020 and $3.56 million in 2021, but could not provide subsidiary listings supporting most of these amounts.

Auditors were also unable to verify an Asset Revaluation Reserve of $6.09 million, while the council had not conducted annual boards of survey to physically verify assets.

The report further revealed the council recorded borrowings from the Fiji Development Bank of $10.37 million in 2019, $10.50 million in 2020 and $10.49 million in 2021.

However, bank audit confirmations and original bank statements were not provided to auditors to verify the balances.

Questions were also raised over operating revenue.

The council reported rates income of $795,455 in 2019, $716,561 in 2020 and $1.23 million in 2021.

The 2019 accounts also contained $6.97 million classified as unidentified revenue.

The Auditor-General said transactions had been recorded directly from bank statements instead of invoices and receipt books, while copies of invoices were unavailable for verification.

The audit consequently could not determine whether adjustments were required to several areas of Nausori Town Council’s financial statements for the three-year period.

item.title: Wellness key to future of Fiji tourism: DPM Gavoka
item.description: Wellness tourism will play an increasingly important role in Fiji’s visitor economy as travellers look beyond traditional beach holidays for experiences that improve their physical and emotional wellbeing, says Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Tourism Viliame Gavoka. Speaking at the opening of the 2026 CIDESCO World Congress in Nadi on Saturday, Mr Gavoka said the changing expectations of in
item.content:encoded:
Wellness tourism will play an increasingly important role in Fiji’s visitor economy as travellers look beyond traditional beach holidays for experiences that improve their physical and emotional wellbeing, says Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Tourism Viliame Gavoka.

Speaking at the opening of the 2026 CIDESCO World Congress in Nadi on Saturday, Mr Gavoka said the changing expectations of international travellers presented Fiji with an opportunity to develop a distinctive wellness tourism industry.

“The traveller has changed. People no longer cross the world only for a beach and a sunset, though we have the finest of both,” Mr Gavoka said.

“They are looking for experiences that can restore them, connect them to a place and leave them feeling better than when they arrived.”

He said Fiji could build its wellness offering around its natural environment, traditional knowledge and renowned hospitality rather than attempting to replicate international spa experiences.

“Fiji can be that destination. Not a copy of a spa you could find anywhere. Fiji itself: our ocean, our gardens, and above all, the hands and knowledge of our people.”

Mr Gavoka said internationally recognised training and certification would also strengthen Fiji’s competitiveness by giving visitors confidence that local therapists met global professional standards.

The Government, he said, regarded wellness as more than simply another tourism marketing product.

“For Government of Fiji, wellness is a real part of our tourism economy, not a line in a brochure,” he said.

“It is part of how we diversify our visitor economy, develop our people, strengthen local supply chains and create experiences that are distinctly ours.”

Mr Gavoka highlighted Nama Fiji’s “Sea to Skin” model as an example of how wellness tourism could generate benefits throughout local communities.

Nama harvested by women in rural communities is transformed into skincare products before being used by professionally trained therapists.

“This is how tourism should work for a small island nation: the value stays here, in our villages and with our people,” he said.

Mr Gavoka said the longer-term ambition was to train a new generation of Fijian therapists, develop internationally competitive spas and salons and encourage young people to regard wellness as a viable career.

The 2026 CIDESCO World Congress is being held in the South Pacific for the first time and coincides with the international organisation’s 80th anniversary.

item.title: Audit unable to verify $1.25m Suva Council cash revenue
item.description: The Auditor-General was unable to determine whether $1.25 million in cash-based revenue collected by the Suva City Council was complete, according to findings in the Report on Municipal Councils recently tabled in Parliament. The issue is among several qualification matters identified in the council’s financial statements for the 2020 financial year.
item.content:encoded:
The Auditor-General was unable to determine whether $1.25 million in cash-based revenue collected by the Suva City Council was complete, according to findings in the Report on Municipal Councils recently tabled in Parliament.

The issue is among several qualification matters identified in the council’s financial statements for the 2020 financial year.

The council recorded $4.08 million in fees, charges and rental income, which included $1.25 million collected from mini markets, stalls, car parks, the swimming pool and public conveniences.

According to the audit report, these revenue streams were collected on a cash basis.

The council had determined it was not practical to maintain controls over the collection of cash from these sources before the money was entered into its financial records.

As a result, auditors were restricted to examining amounts already recorded by the council and could not determine whether all revenue collected had been accounted for.

The report said the audit was therefore “unable to express an opinion whether revenue from these sources reported in the accompanying financial statements was complete.”

Concerns were also raised over $381,988 in inventory recorded by the council as at July 31, 2020.

Auditors were not provided an opportunity to attend the physical inventory count and could not verify the existence, completeness, accuracy or valuation of the stock through alternative means.

The uncertainty also meant auditors could not determine whether adjustments were required to the council’s cost of sales, profit or operating cash flows.

Another significant issue involved $3.81 million in Value Added Tax payable.

The report found the council had not reconciled taxable supplies reported in its VAT returns against revenue recorded in its general ledgers and the Statement of Tax account provided by the Fiji Revenue and Customs Service.

Consequently, auditors were unable to determine whether adjustments were required to either the $3.81 million VAT payable balance or the council’s reported net profit for the 2020 financial year.

item.title: Pacific leaders urged to shield climate talks from fossil fuel influence
item.description: Pacific leaders are being urged to strengthen safeguards against fossil fuel and other vested interests influencing climate negotiations as they gather in Palau ahead of major international climate talks. Transparency International Pacific Chapters made the call ahead of the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting, saying the region must continue demonstrating leadership through transparency, accoun
item.content:encoded:
Pacific leaders are being urged to strengthen safeguards against fossil fuel and other vested interests influencing climate negotiations as they gather in Palau ahead of major international climate talks.

Transparency International Pacific Chapters made the call ahead of the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting, saying the region must continue demonstrating leadership through transparency, accountability and integrity in climate decision-making.

The organisation said Pacific countries were on the frontline of climate change and could not allow private interests to weaken or delay measures needed to protect vulnerable communities.

“For Pacific nations, the stakes are too high to allow vested private interests to weaken or delay action while our communities continue to bear the consequences,” the statement said.

Transparency International said recent international climate negotiations had heightened concerns about the influence of vested interests.

It said that at COP30 in Belém, 54 per cent of participants in national delegations either did not disclose their type of affiliation or identified themselves using broad categories such as “Guest” or “Other”.

“These developments raise an important question: who is shaping climate decisions that determine the future of our communities already facing the impacts of climate change?” it said.

The Pacific chapters want Forum leaders to champion stronger integrity safeguards within the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change process ahead of COP31.

They are calling for a code of conduct for delegates attending pre-COP and COP31 meetings and disclosure of participants’ links to fossil fuel and other high-polluting industries.

The group also wants Australia to demonstrate leadership on integrity ahead of COP31, including through the early establishment of an independent ethics committee.

Transparency International said Pacific leaders had already committed to principles of integrity through regional initiatives including the Teieniwa Vision, 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent and Boe Declaration.

It said those commitments now needed to translate into action within regional and global climate governance.

“We believe Pacific Leaders have both the moral authority and the responsibility to champion these reforms within the UNFCCC at a time when public trust in climate negotiations is under increasing pressure,” the statement said.

“The future of the Blue Pacific depends not only on climate ambition, but on the integrity of the systems that deliver it.”
